title: Basic Approach to Kidney Disease and Renal Artery Stenosis

questions.q: The initial investigation of kidney disease pairs USG abdomen and renal function tests with:
questions.exp: Initial investigation: ultrasonography (USG) abdomen, renal function test (RFT) and urine analysis. (Book p748)

questions.q: For protein estimation in the initial urine analysis, the preferred test is:
questions.exp: Urine analysis: 24hr protein (preferred), albumin/creatinine, protein/creatinine. (Book p748)

questions.q: The RFT arm of the initial investigation measures:
opts: S. urea, S. creatinine, S. Na+ and S. K+
S. urea, S. uric acid, S. Ca2+ and S. Mg2+
S. creatinine, S. albumin, S. Na+ and S. K+
S. urea, S. creatinine, S. ALT and S. AST
questions.exp: RFT: S. urea, S. creatinine, S. Na+, S. K+. (Book p748)

questions.q: On the USG approach, a kidney size below which value points toward chronic kidney disease?
questions.exp: Look for: kidney size <8 cm. (Book p748)

questions.q: Kidneys larger than 10 cm with loss of corticomedullary differentiation are classically seen with:
questions.exp: >10 cm with loss of CMD with: DM, HIV, amyloidosis. (Book p748)

questions.q: Enlarged (>10 cm) kidneys with loss of CMD are listed for all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Loss of CMD with >10 cm kidneys: DM, HIV, amyloidosis; vesicoureteral reflux belongs to the asymmetric-kidney note. (Book p748)

questions.q: Fill up: On the USG approach, seeing corticomedullary differentiation (CMD) places the patient in the ______ arm.
questions.exp: CMD present → CKD; absent → non-CKD. (Book p748)

questions.q: Match each normal-kidney USG structure with its echogenicity — 1) Cortex 2) Pyramids 3) Fat, calyx, sinus, vessels … A) Hyperechoic B) Isoechoic C) Hypoechoic
questions.exp: Isoechoic: cortex; hypoechoic: pyramids; hyperechoic: fat, calyx, sinus, vessels. (Book p748)

questions.q: Which statement about the USG approach is TRUE?
opts: Kidneys of 8-10 cm always retain CMD
Absent CMD places the patient in the CKD arm
USG abdomen is the most important investigation of the approach
Loss of CMD rules out chronic kidney disease
questions.exp: USG abdomen (most important); CMD present → CKD, absent → non-CKD; 8-10 cm loss of CMD is itself a CKD clue. (Book p748)

questions.q: The two end-point branches drawn for established CKD are:
questions.exp: CKD → hemodialysis / transplant. (Book p748)

questions.sec: Initial investigation, USG approach & figures · p748
questions.q: Under 'Urine Analysis' in the initial-investigation flowchart, the box marked (Preferred) sits beside which two boxes?
questions.exp: Urine analysis branches into three printed boxes: 24hr Protein (Preferred), Albumin/Creatinine and Protein/Creatinine — i.e. the ratio tests that supplement the 24-hour collection. (Book p748)

questions.sec: Initial investigation, USG approach & figures · p748
questions.q: The normal-kidney ultrasound figure lists several hyperechoic structures; which of these is NOT in that list?
questions.exp: The labels read Isoechoic: Cortex; Hypoechoic: Pyramid; Hyperechoic: Fat, Calyx, sinus, vessels — the pyramid is the hypoechoic structure. (Book p748)

questions.sec: Initial investigation, USG approach & figures · p748
questions.q: The pair of ultrasound images drawn under 'Chronic Kidney Failure' is captioned 'Cortico medullary differentiation (CMD) lost'.
opts: True — and the same caption also appears under the normal kidney
True — that caption sits below the two failure images
False — the caption is 'Corticomedullary differentiation preserved'
False — the caption belongs to the normal-kidney image
questions.exp: The USG ABDOMEN – In CKD diagram contrasts a normal kidney (with cortex/pyramid labels) against chronic kidney failure images captioned 'Cortico medullary differentiation (CMD) lost'. (Book p748)

questions.sec: Initial investigation, USG approach & figures · p748
questions.q: Fill up: In the 'Look for' list, kidneys measuring 8–10 cm are described by the finding of ______ of CMD.
questions.exp: The three printed size lines are: kidney size <8 cm; 8–10 cm loss of CMD; >10 cm with loss of CMD with DM, HIV, amyloidosis. (Book p748)

questions.sec: Initial investigation, USG approach & figures · p748
questions.q: A 46-year-old with raised creatinine has bilaterally 7.4 cm kidneys on ultrasound. According to the 'Look for' list, this size band:
opts: Is a normal adult kidney length
Is the first entry, below 8 cm, and supports chronic kidney disease
Falls in the 8–10 cm band, so CMD must be assessed first
Falls in the >10 cm band typical of amyloidosis
questions.exp: The first bullet of the look-for list is 'Kidney size <8 cm', which the flowchart uses to place the patient under chronic kidney disease. (Book p748)

questions.sec: Initial investigation, USG approach & figures · p748
questions.q: In the approach flowchart, corticomedullary differentiation marked 'Absent' leads to which label?
questions.exp: As printed, CMD 'Present' runs down to Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and then to Hemodialysis or Transplant, while 'Absent' is routed to Non-CKD — the chart's arrow directions, not the textbook convention, must be quoted here. (Book p748)

questions.q: Before diagnosing CKD on USG one must rule out hydronephroureteronephrosis, whose clue on imaging is:
opts: Calyces becoming prominent and ureter seen
questions.exp: Rule out hydronephroureteronephrosis before diagnosing CKD; calyces becoming prominent and ureter seen. (Book p749)

questions.q: Match each tempo with its non-CKD category — 1) Hours to days 2) Days to weeks 3) Normal RFT with renal disease … A) Acute kidney injury (AKI) B) Rapidly progressive renal failure (RPRF) C) Nephrotic syn / RTA type I-II / asymptomatic urine abnormality
questions.exp: Hours to days → AKI; days to weeks → RPRF; normal RFT with renal disease → nephrotic syn, RTA I/II, asymptomatic urine abnormality. (Book p749)

questions.q: The AKI arm of the flowchart lists postrenal, ATN, AIN and:
opts: Pre-renal investigation with normal urine analysis
questions.exp: AKI: postrenal (B/L hydronephroureteronephrosis on USG), pre-renal (normal urine analysis), ATN, AIN. (Book p749)

questions.q: Which statement about the AKI arm is TRUE?
opts: B/L hydronephroureteronephrosis defines the pre-renal category
The pre-renal category is expected to show a normal urine analysis
The postrenal category shows a normal USG
ATN and AIN are postrenal causes
questions.exp: Pre-renal investigation: normal urine analysis; postrenal: B/L hydronephroureteronephrosis (USG). (Book p749)

questions.sec: CKD mimics & the AKI arm · p749
questions.q: Fill up: In the hours-to-days AKI list, ATN is expanded on this page as acute tubular ______.
questions.exp: The printed lines are 'Acute tubular nephrosis (ATN)' and 'Acute interstitial nephrosis (AIN)' — the page uses nephrosis for both, unlike the usual nephritis wording seen elsewhere in the notes. (Book p749)

questions.sec: CKD mimics & the AKI arm · p749
questions.q: The postrenal line of the AKI branch reads B/L hydroureteronephrosis with USG written in brackets.
opts: True — ultrasound is the study named against postrenal AKI
False — the bracketed investigation is CT abdomen
False — the line names retrograde pyelography
True — and the same line adds 'diagnosed with biopsy'
questions.exp: Printed: 'Postrenal : B/L hydroureteronephrosis (USG)'; the biopsy line belongs to RPGN in the days-to-weeks branch. (Book p749)

questions.q: Rapidly progressive renal failure most commonly turns out to be:
questions.exp: RPRF → RPGN (m/c), diagnosed with biopsy; severe ATN and TMA are rare causes. (Book p749)

questions.q: All of the following appear under rapidly progressive renal failure in the flowchart EXCEPT:
questions.exp: RPRF: RPGN (m/c), severe ATN, TMA; nephrotic syndrome sits under normal RFT with renal disease. (Book p749)

questions.q: Match each item of the hypertensive-crisis branch with its label — 1) Renal artery stenosis 2) Thrombotic microangiopathy 3) Hypertensive crisis … A) Small vessel kidney disease B) Large vessel kidney disease C) Vascular cause
questions.exp: Hypertensive crisis: vascular cause; RAS = large vessel kidney disease; TMA = small vessel kidney disease. (Book p749)

questions.q: Normal RFT with renal disease includes nephrotic syndrome, asymptomatic urine abnormality and:
questions.exp: Normal RFT with renal disease: nephrotic syn, renal tubular acidosis type I/II, asymptomatic urine abnormality. (Book p749)

questions.q: Renal artery stenosis is also known as:
opts: Renovascular HTN (RVH) / renal artery occlusion disease (RAOD)
questions.exp: AKA renovascular HTN (RVH) / renal artery occlusion disease (RAOD). (Book p749)

questions.q: Left untreated, renal artery stenosis can progress to:
questions.exp: Can progress to CKD / ischemic nephropathy. (Book p749)

questions.q: Which vessel-size statement is TRUE as per the flowchart?
opts: Both TMA and RAS are large vessel diseases
TMA is a small vessel kidney disease while RAS is a large vessel kidney disease
TMA is a large vessel kidney disease while RAS is a small vessel kidney disease
Both TMA and RAS are small vessel diseases
questions.exp: RAS: large vessel kidney disease; TMA: small vessel kidney disease. (Book p749)

questions.sec: RPRF, vascular causes & RAS introduction · p749
questions.q: In the days-to-weeks branch, the bracket 'Rare cause' is drawn against which two entries?
questions.exp: Under rapidly progressive renal failure the list is RPGN (m/c, diagnosed with biopsy), then severe ATN and TMA grouped by a bracket labelled 'Rare cause'. (Book p749)

questions.sec: RPRF, vascular causes & RAS introduction · p749
questions.q: A 32-year-old has creatinine rising from 1.2 to 5.0 mg/dL in ten days with an active sediment and 2+ proteinuria. Following the non-CKD flowchart, the picture is:
opts: Normal RFT with renal disease — asymptomatic urine abnormality
Hypertensive crisis — vascular cause, so screen for renal artery stenosis
Days to weeks tempo — rapidly progressive renal failure, with RPGN the m/c cause and biopsy the confirmation
Hours to days tempo — pre-renal AKI with normal urine analysis
questions.exp: The 'Days to weeks' arm carries rapidly progressive renal failure whose m/c cause is RPGN, diagnosed with biopsy; the tempo and the active sediment exclude the pre-renal and vascular arms. (Book p749)

questions.q: Match each population with its most common cause of RAS — 1) Overall 2) Young population 3) Indian/Asian population … A) Takayasu arteritis B) Atherosclerosis C) Fibromuscular dysplasia
questions.exp: Overall: atherosclerosis; young population: fibromuscular dysplasia; Indian/Asian: Takayasu arteritis. (Book p750)

questions.q: In young males, the cause of RAS that involves the entire length of the renal artery with microaneurysms is:
questions.exp: Young males: polyarteritis nodosa – entire length renal artery – microaneurysm. (Book p750)

questions.q: Atherosclerotic RAS involves the proximal renal artery over 1-2 cm and becomes symptomatic beyond what occlusion?
questions.exp: Atherosclerosis: proximal renal artery (1-2 cm); symptomatic: >80% occlusion. (Book p750)

questions.q: Fill up: Fibromuscular dysplasia, the young-population cause, affects the ______ renal artery.
questions.exp: Fibromuscular dysplasia (arteriopathy): mid to distal renal artery. (Book p750)

questions.q: The female-to-male ratio written for Takayasu arteritis is:
questions.exp: Takayasu arteritis (F:M = 9:1), proximal renal artery. (Book p750)

questions.q: The types of RAS are explained by the Goldblatt:
questions.exp: Explain by Goldblatt: two kidney one clip model. (Book p750)

questions.q: The pathogenesis of unilateral RAS starts with the clue:
questions.exp: Unilateral RAS pathogenesis: asymmetric kidney size. (Book p750)

questions.q: The written vasoconstriction potency order is:
questions.exp: Vasoconstriction potency: urotension > endothelin > AT-II. (Book p750)

questions.q: The clinical feature and basic investigation picture of unilateral RAS are:
opts: Flash pulmonary edema with raised S. creatinine
Persistent HTN with RFT and urine analysis in the normal range
Persistent HTN with abnormal urine analysis
questions.exp: C/F: persistent HTN; basic investigation (RFT, urine analysis) normal range. (Book p750)

questions.q: In the affected kidney of unilateral RAS, the sequence after reduced RBF/perfusion is:
opts: Renin angiotensin system → ↑ aldosterone → ↑ AT-II → profound vasoconstriction → ↑ BP
questions.exp: Affected kidney: ↓ RBF/perfusion → (+) renin angiotensin → (+) ↑ aldosterone → ↑ AT-II ↑↑ → profound vasoconstriction → ↑ BP → HTN/HTN crisis. (Book p750)

questions.q: Fill up: In the normal kidney, ↑ renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure reduces reabsorption from the ______, producing pressure natriuresis.
questions.exp: Normal kidney: ↑ RIHP → ↓ reabsorption from PCT → ↑ excretion of Na+/H2O (pressure natriuresis theory). (Book p750)

questions.q: Which statement about the normal (contralateral) kidney in unilateral RAS is TRUE?
opts: It shows ↑ renal blood flow/medullary flow with ↑ RIHP
It shows ↓ renal blood flow and activated renin
It reabsorbs more sodium from the PCT
questions.exp: Normal kidney: ↑ RBF/medullary flow → ↑ RIHP → ↓ PCT reabsorption → ↑ Na+/H2O excretion. (Book p750)

questions.q: The book's note lists asymmetric kidney in vesicoureteral reflux and renal artery stenosis; it is NOT listed for:
questions.exp: Asymmetric kidney seen in: vesicoureteral reflux; renal artery stenosis. (Book p750)

questions.q: In the affected kidney, the doubly-raised AT-II produces:
opts: Profound vasoconstriction with rising blood pressure
questions.exp: ↑ Angiotensin II (AT-II) ↑↑ → profound vasoconstriction → ↑ blood pressure → HTN/HTN crisis. (Book p750)

questions.q: Of the four 'most common' branches, which two both name the proximal renal artery as the site?
questions.exp: Site lines: atherosclerosis — proximal renal artery (1–2 cm); Takayasu — proximal renal artery; fibromuscular dysplasia — mid to distal; polyarteritis nodosa — entire length. (Book p750)

questions.q: Fill up: The page puts the word ______ in brackets after fibromuscular dysplasia, classifying it as a disease of the arterial wall.
questions.exp: The young-population branch reads 'Fibromuscular dysplasia (Arteriopathy) — mid to distal renal artery'. (Book p750)

questions.q: In the affected-kidney chain, the arrows carrying a '(+)' mark are the ones running into the renin–angiotensin system box and into the aldosterone box.
opts: False — only the arrow into the renin–angiotensin system is marked
False — the '(+)' marks appear on the normal-kidney side
True — and a third '(+)' marks the arrow into profound vasoconstriction
True — both '(+)' arrows denote stimulation of the next step
questions.exp: The printed chain is ↓RBF/perfusion →(+) renin angiotensin system →(+) ↑aldosterone → ↑angiotensin II (↑↑) → profound vasoconstriction → ↑BP → HTN/HTN crisis. (Book p750)

questions.q: A 26-year-old Indian woman with weak upper-limb pulses and severe hypertension is found to have a renal artery bruit. Which branch of the 'most common' tree fits her?
opts: Polyarteritis nodosa — entire length with microaneurysms
Takayasu arteritis — proximal renal artery, F:m 9:1
Fibromuscular dysplasia — mid to distal artery
questions.exp: The Indian/Asian population branch is Takayasu arteritis with the F:m ratio printed as 9:1 and the proximal renal artery affected; FMD belongs to the general young population and PAN to young males. (Book p750)

questions.q: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis becomes symptomatic once occlusion passes:
questions.exp: The overall branch reads 'Symptomatic: >80% occlusion' of the proximal 1–2 cm of the renal artery. (Book p750)

questions.q: On USG the radiological clue for RAS is asymmetric kidney; the screening test is:
questions.exp: On USG: asymmetric kidney; screening test: renal doppler. (Book p751)

questions.q: The investigation of choice to confirm renal artery stenosis is:
opts: CT renal angio or MR angiography
questions.exp: IOC: CT renal angio or MR angiography (confirms the doppler screen). (Book p751)

questions.q: The drug of choice written for unilateral RAS is:
questions.exp: Treatment: ACE inhibitors / ARBs – (DOC). (Book p751)

questions.q: Percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty (PTRA) is offered only if the kidney size is above:
questions.exp: PTRA – only if kidney size > 8 cm. (Book p751)

questions.q: The pair of CT/MR angiogram images drawn to the right of the renal doppler picture carries which caption?
questions.exp: The two panels (A and B, each with a white arrow) are captioned 'unilateral renal artery stenosis'; the separate caption 'Bilateral renal artery stenosis' belongs to the aortogram lower on the page. (Book p751)

questions.q: An 8 cm left kidney is normal and the right, stenosed kidney measures 6.5 cm; blood pressure is controlled on ramipril. Per the treatment block, angioplasty is:
opts: Not offered, because PTRA is reserved for bilateral disease
Not offered, because PTRA is listed only if kidney size is greater than 8 cm
Offered at once, since the stenosis is unilateral
Offered only after a trial of diuretics
questions.exp: The unilateral treatment block lists ACE inhibitors/ARBs (DOC) and PTRA '- Only if kidney size > 8 cm'; the 6.5 cm kidney fails that condition. (Book p751)

questions.q: Match each drug class with where the page calls it the drug of choice — 1) ACE inhibitors/ARBs 2) Diuretics … A) Blood pressure in bilateral RAS B) Unilateral RAS C) Neither, both are contraindicated in RAS
questions.exp: ACE inhibitors/ARBs are DOC in unilateral RAS but contraindicated in bilateral RAS (they ↓GFR), where diuretics take over as the DOC for blood pressure. (Book p751)

questions.q: The prognosis written for bilateral RAS is:
opts: Responsive to PTRA alone without stenting
questions.exp: Bilateral RAS: poor prognosis. (Book p751)

questions.q: In bilateral RAS, loss of pressure natriuresis with ↓ RIHP leads to:
opts: ↑ Na+/H2O retention → intravascular volume overload → recurrent flash pulmonary edema
Sustained renin activation without volume change
questions.exp: Loss of pressure natriuresis / ↓ RIHP → ↑ Na+/H2O retention → intravascular volume overload → recurrent flash pulmonary edema (d/t intravascular edema). (Book p751)

questions.q: Which statement about the bilateral RAS diagram is TRUE?
opts: The renin angiotensin system stays maximally stimulated without feedback
Pressure natriuresis is preserved in both kidneys
Intravascular volume overload feeds back negatively on the renin angiotensin system
questions.exp: The (−) arrow shows intravascular volume overload inhibiting the renin angiotensin system. (Book p751)

questions.q: Recurrent flash pulmonary edema in bilateral RAS is treated with:
opts: B/L percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty with stenting
questions.exp: Rx: B/L percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty with stenting. (Book p751)

questions.q: For blood pressure control in bilateral RAS, the book lists diuretics as DOC while ACE inhibitors/ARBs are:
questions.exp: In BP: diuretics (DOC); ACE inhibitors / ARBs: C/I as they ↓ GFR. (Book p751)

questions.q: All of the following are listed in the bilateral RAS treatment block EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Listed: diuretics (DOC), stop smoking, start statins; ACEi/ARBs are C/I. (Book p751)

questions.q: In the bilateral pathogenesis drawing, both arteries carry a red cross and the legend beside it reads 'x – Occlusion'.
opts: True — the crosses stand for occlusion on either side
False — the crosses mark the clip used in the unilateral model
False — only one artery is crossed in the bilateral drawing
True — and the same legend defines 'x' as a stenosis of less than 80%
questions.exp: The unilateral drawing shows a clip on one limb, whereas the bilateral drawing crosses both limbs and prints the red legend 'x – Occlusion', explaining why neither kidney can escape the low perfusion. (Book p751)

questions.q: The flowchart attributes recurrent flash pulmonary edema in bilateral renal artery stenosis to:
opts: Intravascular edema, written in brackets after the phrase
Low oncotic pressure from nephrotic syndrome
questions.exp: Printed line: 'Recurrent flash pulmonary edema (D/t intravascular edema)', reached from ↑Na+/H2O retention and intravascular volume overload, and treated with B/L PTRA with stenting. (Book p751)

questions.q: Besides blood-pressure control, which pair of general measures appears under treatment of bilateral renal artery stenosis?
opts: Start ACE inhibitors and restrict protein
Begin dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulate
questions.exp: The treatment block lists In BP → diuretics (DOC) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs contraindicated as they ↓GFR, followed by 'Stop smoking' and 'Start statins'. (Book p751)

questions.q: A smoker with bilateral RAS and an ejection fraction of 60% returns with two episodes of overnight breathlessness; CDU confirms bilateral stenosis. The page's sequence predicts the episodes are due to:
opts: Rise in RIHP driving natriuresis, managed by an ACE inhibitor
Arteriopathy of fibromuscular dysplasia, managed by PTRA alone
Medullary hypoxia, managed by statins and smoking cessation
Intravascular volume overload from loss of pressure natriuresis, managed by B/L PTRA with stenting
questions.exp: Bilateral occlusion removes the pressure-natriuresis escape (↓RIHP → ↑Na+/H2O retention → volume overload → recurrent flash pulmonary edema), for which the flowchart's Rx is B/L percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty with stenting; statins and stopping smoking are the additional measures. (Book p751)

questions.q: The book's caution while interpreting flash pulmonary edema in this context is:
opts: Every pulmonary edema is cardiac unless proven otherwise
Every pulmonary edema is renal unless proven otherwise
Flash pulmonary edema excludes cardiac disease
Pulmonary edema never occurs in bilateral RAS
questions.exp: Note: every pulmonary edema is cardiac unless proven otherwise. (Book p752)

questions.q: The screening test named on this page is renal artery stenosis colour doppler ultrasound (CDU); its characteristic waveform clue is the:
questions.exp: Screening test: RAS colour doppler ultrasound (CDU); look for parvus tardus pattern. (Book p752)

questions.q: On CDU, a resistivity index (RI) at or above which value points to parenchymal disease (CKD)?
questions.exp: RI ≥ 0.8 → parenchymal disease: CKD. (Book p752)

questions.q: With RI < 0.8, the stenosis criteria that route the patient to CT/MR renal angiography are:
opts: Peak systolic velocity > 100 cm/s OR RAR > 2.5 OR ΔRI > 0.01
Peak systolic velocity > 250 cm/s OR RAR > 5 OR ΔRI > 0.1
Peak systolic velocity > 180 mm/s OR RAR > 3.5 OR ΔRI > 0.5
Peak systolic velocity > 180 cm/s OR RAR > 3.5 OR ΔRI > 0.05
questions.exp: RI < 0.8 with PSV > 180 cm/s OR RAR > 3.5 OR ΔRI > 0.05 → CT/MR renal angiography (IOC). (Book p752)

questions.q: All of the following are CDU look-for criteria of RAS EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The book's velocity criterion is peak systolic velocity > 180 cm/s, not 80 cm/s. (Book p752)

questions.q: The IOC after a positive screen is CT/MR renal angiography; the gold standard that is both diagnostic and therapeutic is:
questions.exp: Conventional angiograph (gold standard): diagnostic and therapeutic. (Book p752)

questions.q: Which statement about fibromuscular dysplasia is TRUE?
opts: It is an inflammatory vasculitis of the proximal aorta
It is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arteriopathy most common in young girls
It is an atherosclerotic disease of elderly males
questions.exp: Non atherosclerotic/non inflammatory arteriopathy; incident: m/c in young girls. (Book p752)

questions.q: The pathology of fibromuscular dysplasia is medial fibroplasia in the tunica media of the:
questions.exp: Involves middle to distal renal artery: medial fibroplasia in tunica media. (Book p752)

questions.q: Fibromuscular dysplasia is bilateral in the renal arteries in 25% of cases; the other 25% involve:
questions.exp: 25% B/L renal artery, 25% involves cerebral vessels. (Book p752)

questions.q: The angiographic feature illustrated for medial fibromuscular dysplasia is the:
questions.exp: The "string of beads" feature in medial fibromuscular dysplasia. (Book p752)

questions.q: The treatment of choice for fibromuscular dysplasia, carrying a good prognosis, is:
questions.exp: Treatment: PTRA (good prognosis). (Book p752)

questions.q: Which caption is printed beneath the first pair of angiograms at the top of this page?
opts: Stents in renal artery bifurcation stenosis
questions.exp: The first two images are captioned 'Stents in renal artery bifurcation stenosis'; the round pre-op/post-op pair carries 'Severe stenosis' and 'Good flow', and the beaded angiogram below belongs to fibromuscular dysplasia. (Book p752)

questions.q: The two round fluoroscopy images are headed 'Pre-op' and 'Post-op' and captioned 'Severe stenosis' and 'Good flow' respectively.
opts: True — the pair documents the angiographic result before and after intervention
False — both images are labelled pre-operative
False — the captions read 'mild stenosis' and 'no flow'
True — and the same figure is captioned 'string of beads'
questions.exp: The heading row prints Pre-op over the first image and Post-op over the second, with the captions 'Severe stenosis' and 'Good flow' under them. (Book p752)

questions.q: Along with peak systolic velocity above 180 cm/s and RAR above 3.5, the colour doppler criteria accept a change in resistivity index greater than:
questions.exp: The RI < 0.8 arm reads: Peak systolic velocity > 180 cm/s OR RAR > 3.5 OR ΔRI > 0.05, all routing to CT/MR renal angiography. (Book p752)

questions.q: Fill up: When the colour doppler study is labelled 'Investigation inconclusive', the flowchart sends the patient for ______.
questions.exp: Both the RI ≥ 0.8 side path 'Investigation inconclusive' and the RI < 0.8 positive-criteria path converge on CT/MR renal angiography, marked (IOC). (Book p752)

questions.q: Fill up: Under 'Incident', fibromuscular dysplasia is stated to be most common in ______.
questions.exp: The FMD block reads: Non atherosclerotic/non inflammatory Arteriopathy; Incident: m/c in young girls; pathology — middle to distal renal artery, medial fibroplasia in tunica media; 25% B/L renal artery and 25% cerebral vessels; Treatment: PTRA (good prognosis). (Book p752)

units.title: Initial investigation & the USG approach
units.guide: Three arms — USG abdomen (the most important investigation), RFT (urea, creatinine, Na+, K+) and urine analysis (24 hr protein preferred, plus albumin and protein ratios). Look for size <8 cm, 8–10 cm with loss of CMD, and >10 cm with loss of CMD in DM/HIV/amyloidosis; the normal-kidney figure labels cortex isoechoic, pyramid hypoechoic and fat/calyx/sinus/vessels hyperechoic.

units.title: CKD mimics: hydronephroureteronephrosis & the AKI arm
units.guide: Rule out hydronephroureteronephrosis before diagnosing CKD (prominent calyces, visible ureter). The hours-to-days tempo is AKI: postrenal B/L hydroureteronephrosis (USG), pre-renal with normal urine analysis, and the page's 'acute tubular/interstitial nephrosis'.

units.title: Rapidly progressive failure, vascular causes & RAS words
units.guide: Days to weeks = RPRF (RPGN m/c, biopsy; severe ATN and TMA bracketed as rare causes); hypertensive crisis = vascular: RAS (large vessel) and TMA (small vessel); normal RFT with renal disease = nephrotic syndrome, RTA I/II, asymptomatic urine abnormality. RAS is also renovascular hypertension/renal artery occlusion disease and progresses to ischemic nephropathy.

units.title: RAS: who gets what, and the Goldblatt model
units.guide: Overall atherosclerosis (proximal 1–2 cm, symptomatic >80%); young population FMD/arteriopathy (mid to distal); Indian/Asian Takayasu (proximal, F:m 9:1); young males PAN (entire length, microaneurysm). Types are explained by the Goldblatt two kidney one clip model.

units.title: Unilateral RAS: pathogenesis of the small kidney
units.guide: Asymmetric kidney size (also seen in reflux). Affected side: ↓RBF →(+) RAS →(+) aldosterone → ↑↑AT-II → profound vasoconstriction → HTN/HTN crisis, with persistent hypertension and normal RFT/urine. Contralateral side: ↑RBF/medullary flow → ↑RIHP → ↓PCT reabsorption → natriuresis (pressure natriuresis theory). Potency order: urotensin > endothelin > AT-II.

units.title: Diagnosing RAS and treating unilateral disease
units.guide: USG clue is an asymmetric kidney; screening = renal doppler; confirm with CT renal angiography or MR angiography (IOC), the captioned figure being 'unilateral renal artery stenosis'. Treatment: ACE inhibitors/ARBs are DOC; PTRA only if the kidney is >8 cm.

units.title: Bilateral RAS: volume overload, flash edema & treatment
units.guide: Poor prognosis. Both arteries are crossed ('x – Occlusion'); ↓RBF raises renin but the natriuresis escape is lost (↓RIHP), so Na+/water retention → intravascular volume overload → recurrent flash pulmonary edema (d/t intravascular edema) → B/L PTRA with stenting. For BP: diuretics are DOC, ACE inhibitors/ARBs are contraindicated (↓GFR); stop smoking, start statins.

units.title: Colour doppler cut-offs, angiography & fibromuscular dysplasia
units.guide: Every pulmonary edema is cardiac until proven otherwise. CDU looks for parvus tardus and RI: ≥0.8 = parenchymal disease/CKD; <0.8 with PSV >180 cm/s, RAR >3.5 or ΔRI >0.05 → CT/MR angiography (IOC), also for inconclusive studies; conventional angiography is the gold standard and is both diagnostic and therapeutic. FMD: young girls, non-atherosclerotic non-inflammatory arteriopathy, middle–distal artery, medial fibroplasia, 25% bilateral renal and 25% cerebral, string of beads, treated by PTRA with good prognosis.
